title: NWS spring river outlooks put 90-day crests outside their 5-95% stage range 1.6 times as often as stated at 655 US gauges in 2008-2026; wetter weather explains about one third of high misses
abstract: We tested the probabilistic river outlooks (product ESF) that 34 NWS offices issued in January-May 2008-2026 against observed 90-day crests. We parsed 3,619 outlooks, matched forecast points to 655 USGS gauges, checked the NWS stage datum against USGS gauge height for each gauge and year, and scored 42,787 stage-quantile forecasts and 37,015 flood-category forecasts. The test plan was written before outcomes were joined. Crests were above the highest listed stage 1.74 times (95% CI 1.31-2.29, year bootstrap) and below the lowest listed stage 1.53 times (1.27-1.82) as often as stated; the 5-95% range held 83.4% of crests, not 90%. The outlooks use Ensemble Streamflow Prediction (ESP), which samples past weather but treats model states as known. Basin precipitation during the outlooks was skewed toward the wet end of the 1949-2018 trace climate; reweighting forecasts to uniform weather lowered the upper ratio to 1.46 (1.19-1.77), so at least about 38% of the upper excess comes from wetter weather, and raised the lower ratio to 1.76. The remaining misses depend on a gap visible at issue time: when the river was already more than 2 ft above the outlook floor, upper misses were 3.7 times the stated rate; when the outlook expected a rise of more than 2 ft with 95% certainty, lower misses were 2.8 times the stated rate and held all net lower excess. Flood-category chances were near calibrated in total (O/E minor 1.15, moderate 1.07, major 0.78) but over-confident at the ends: minor flooding followed 5.8% of '<5%' forecasts and major flooding 55% of forecasts with 65% or more. Current-condition chances beat normal-condition chances (Brier skill 0.05-0.08). Limitations: forecasts are strongly dependent within years (about 19 effective years), 29% of table rows had no matched USGS gauge, the weather proxy is monthly basin precipitation, and two tests were added as dated amendments.
